name: Coffee for skin / Cold brew

lead: Appearance communities promote coffee and cold brew, drunk or applied topically, for healthier-looking skin and looks in general.

Cold brew is made by steeping coarse grounds in cold or room-temperature water for about 4 to 24 hours and has lower titratable acidity than hot coffee. A 2017 umbrella review found coffee generally safe at usual intakes. The sources reviewed do not address skin, topical use, cellulite or under-eye effects of coffee.

paras: People drink coffee or cold brew daily, and some use coffee grounds or cold brew as a topical scrub or under-eye treatment. It is usually part of a wider skincare or diet routine.
Caffeine can cause anxiety or sleep disruption at high intakes, and pregnancy limits apply.

web.title: PubMed search results: topical caffeine and coffee for skin

angle.text: Appearance communities drink coffee and cold brew, or apply it topically, aiming for healthier-looking skin. Coffee has general safety and health research behind it; skin effects have not been studied in the sources reviewed.

lead: Coffee for skin refers to using coffee, including cold brew, to look better: drunk for its antioxidants and a perceived effect on skin aging, or applied as caffeine-containing creams, serums and coffee scrubs aimed at puffiness, dark circles and the look of cellulite [1][1].

Caffeine is increasingly used in cosmetics because it is biologically active and can penetrate the skin barrier; a 2013 review in Skin Pharmacology and Physiology describes topical formulations that typically contain about 3% caffeine [1]. Dermatology literature also discusses caffeine and coffee in sunscreens and other topicals [1].

Cold brew is made by steeping coarse grounds in cold or room-temperature water for roughly 4 to 24 hours and has lower titratable acidity than hot coffee [2]. Studies of its antioxidant extraction compared with hot brew exist [3]. On T Nation, cold brew comes up as an energy-drink alternative rather than as a skin product [4].

Spent coffee grounds, the leftover from hot or cold brewing, contain caffeine, chlorogenic acids, trigonelline, polyphenols and melanoidins like the beverage itself, and are the base of coffee scrubs and masks; a review of their uses focuses on food and waste reduction rather than cosmetics [5].

paras: Caffeine-containing creams, serums and gels are marketed for eye-area puffiness, skin firming and cellulite, and coffee-extract ingredients are used for antioxidant and anti-aging claims [1][1]. Researchers have also tested caffeine-loaded gels for cellulite using delivery aids such as sonophoresis [1].
Some people drink coffee for its polyphenols as part of a skin-aging or photoprotection routine; surveys and epidemiological analyses of coffee intake and skin condition exist [1].

Cold brew is made by steeping coarsely ground coffee in cold or room-temperature water, with time rather than heat driving extraction; steeping typically runs 4 to 24 hours and yields a dense concentrate [2]. Cold water extracts fewer of the acidic oils found in hot-brewed coffee, which is linked to lower titratable acidity and reduced astringency, and caffeine extracts more slowly in cold water than in hot [2].

A 2023 review of cold and hot brew antioxidants reports that most cold brew protocols immerse grounds in water at or below room temperature for several hours, that higher brewing temperature or longer brewing time generally yielded greater antioxidant activity, and that lighter roasts yielded greater antioxidant activity in most studies [3]. Because antioxidant content depends on roast, grind, temperature and time, cold and hot coffee can differ in what they deliver [3].

Food-safety research notes that cold brew can pose a risk for bacterial pathogens if stored improperly; a 2023 study found pathogens spiked into unprocessed cold brew were still detectable after 60 days at 4 C and 90 days at 23 C, while high-pressure processing reduced them by more than 6 logs [6].

sections.h: History of cold and iced coffee
paras: Cold coffee drinks have a long record. The sweetened Algerian drink mazagran dates to around 1840 and is called by locals the original iced coffee, and frozen coffee drinks resembling slush, such as Italy's granita al caffe, are documented in the nineteenth century [7]. Coffee brewed hot and then chilled with ice appeared on menus and in recipes in the late nineteenth century [7].

In Japan, iced coffee has been served in coffeehouses since the Taisho period, around the 1920s, typically with gum syrup and milk, and cold-brewed coffee there is known as Dutch coffee, a name tied to the historic Dutch coffee trade from Indonesia [7]. In 1969 UCC Ueshima Coffee released canned coffee, making coffee widely available [7]. In the United States, a 1920 campaign by the Joint Coffee Trade Publicity Committee is credited with popularising iced coffee, and later chains including Dunkin' Donuts, McDonald's, Burger King and Starbucks marketed it; Starbucks has used a double-strength hot-brew method rather than cold brew so melted ice does not dilute the drink [7].

Cosmetic caffeine is described as biologically active and able to penetrate the skin barrier, usually formulated at around 3 percent in creams and serums [1]. Marketing links it to temporary tightening, reduced under-eye puffiness and a smoother look in cellulite-prone areas; researchers have tested caffeine gels with delivery aids such as sonophoresis [1]. Dermatology literature also discusses caffeine and coffee in sunscreens and other topicals [1]. Coffee scrubs made from spent grounds use the ground particles for mechanical exfoliation while delivering coffee compounds present in the grounds, such as caffeine and polyphenols [5].

Wikipedia's cellulite article lists massage, suction, energy-based devices and injectables as treatments and says cellulite can resist many treatments, without giving evidence for caffeine creams specifically [8]. Spent coffee grounds from hot or cold brewing are the usual base of coffee scrubs, and a review of their properties describes caffeine, chlorogenic acids and other compounds still present after brewing [5].

Coffee is associated with lower all-cause and cardiovascular mortality and lower type 2 diabetes risk, with possible increased fracture risk in women and pregnancy concerns [9]. A 2014 meta-analysis linked 4 cups a day with 16 percent lower all-cause mortality, and unfiltered coffee can raise LDL cholesterol [9][9]. Health authorities cite about 400 mg of caffeine a day (roughly five cups) as an intake that raises no safety concerns for healthy adults, and lower limits for pregnancy [10][9].

Caffeine is a competitive antagonist of adenosine receptors; side effects in some people include anxiety, jitteriness, insomnia and, at high doses, palpitations, and regular users can experience brief withdrawal headaches [10]. Doses above about 300 mg can cause or worsen anxiety in some people [9]. These effects are relevant to appearance only indirectly, for example through sleep.

Reviews cited by Wikipedia report that a 2017 umbrella review found coffee generally safe at usual intake and more likely to benefit than harm at three to four cups a day, that the European Society of Cardiology said in 2021 that three to four cups is probably not harmful and may be mildly beneficial, and that the American Heart Association said in 2026 that up to about five cups (roughly 400 mg caffeine) a day was safe over adult life [9]. The IARC evaluation in 2016 found no conclusive evidence that coffee is carcinogenic but reported that very hot beverages probably cause oesophageal cancer [9].

sections.h: How people use it for their looks
paras: Coffee enters appearance routines in three main ways. Caffeine-containing eye creams and serums are applied in the morning with the aim of a less puffy, more awake-looking under-eye area; caffeinated body gels and creams are used on thighs and hips with the aim of a smoother look in cellulite-prone areas; and homemade or store-bought coffee scrubs, made from used grounds mixed with an oil or other base, are massaged onto the body as a mild exfoliant.[1] Drinking coffee, including cold brew, is discussed separately as a source of antioxidant polyphenols such as chlorogenic acids that people hope will support skin as they age.[3]

Cold brew specifically appeals to some drinkers because it tastes less acidic and bitter than hot coffee, and the cold-extracted concentrate is easy to dilute and keep in the fridge, so it has become a routine daily drink for people who also care about training and appearance.[2]

A cup of coffee contains caffeine, a methylxanthine alkaloid, along with chlorogenic acids, trigonelline, melanoidins and other polyphenols; a 6-ounce cup typically holds roughly 50 to 175 mg of caffeine depending on bean, roast and preparation.[10] Cold water extracts caffeine and the bitter catechins more slowly than hot water, so brew time, grind and ratio matter for how much ends up in the cup, and a 2023 review notes that most antioxidant studies compare cold and hot brew under varying protocols.[2][3]

The same compounds are the reason coffee is used topically. Cosmetic chemists include caffeine because it is biologically active and reported to penetrate the skin barrier, and a 2013 review sets out its mechanisms of action and its proposed cosmetic roles, which marketing ties to de-puffing and to the look of cellulite.[1]

sections.h: Caffeine, sleep and the rested look
paras: Caffeine's half-life in healthy adults is about 3 to 7 hours, shorter in smokers and roughly doubled in women taking oral contraceptives, and it can delay or prevent sleep; for some people as little as 100 mg a day may keep disrupting sleep [10]. Because sleep affects how rested the face looks, people who drink coffee for its skin or energy benefits often discuss timing it earlier in the day, a practice that appears in training communities rather than in clinical guidance [10][4].

Mild physical dependence and withdrawal symptoms such as headache, fatigue and irritability can occur with more than 100 mg a day and typically last no more than a day or so; Wikipedia notes that only about half of people who report withdrawal show it in laboratory tests [10]. For pregnancy, the UK Food Standards Agency advises under 200 mg a day, ACOG considers up to 200 mg a day safe, Health Canada gives a limit of 300 mg a day, and EFSA says up to 200 mg a day raises no concerns; the evidence is described as inconclusive [10].

Drunk coffee carries the usual caffeine considerations: health authorities cited on Wikipedia describe about 400 mg a day as an intake not associated with safety concerns for healthy adults, with lower limits advised in pregnancy.[10][9] T Nation members describe the practical side of this, including a user who reported a caffeine headache after two glasses of cold brew when they had been off caffeine for a while.[4] Cold brew sold ready-to-drink has been studied for microbial safety when stored improperly, and high-pressure processing has been tested to extend its shelf life.[6]

As with any cosmetic, irritation or sensitivity to fragrance or added oils is possible with topical coffee products, and coffee scrub grains are coarse, so these products are mostly marketed for the body rather than the face.

A 2013 review describes caffeine's mechanisms of action and cosmetic use, noting it penetrates the skin barrier and is typically formulated near 3% [1]. A 2022 clinical study of a coffee pulp supplement reported that after four weeks skin brightness, elasticity, spotting and collagen content were slightly better than baseline (p < 0.05) [1]. A 2024 Mendelian randomization analysis examined coffee and other beverages in relation to facial skin aging, and a 2015 cross-sectional survey looked at coffee and polyphenol intake and skin photoprotection in Japanese women [1]. A 2026 review in Antioxidants summarises coffee-derived materials as showing multifunctional value against skin aging, inflammation and barrier dysfunction [1].

Studies of coffee compounds in general include research on spent coffee grounds in rats and humans (improved metabolic parameters and gut microbiome with hot-brew grounds), which concerns metabolic health rather than skin [5].
No published trials of cold brew specifically for skin were located.

lore.intro: Coffee for skin is discussed less as a skin treatment than as part of daily routines: on T Nation and Hacker News cold brew appears as a stimulant drink and an energy-drink alternative, while beauty media discuss coffee scrubs and caffeine creams.[11][12]
